friction.detail: The reported gate failure was not a source defect. `standards-typescript test:unit` reported 1077/1077 tests passing with zero assertion failures; two suites failed to *run* because their jest workers were killed by SIGSEGV — `common/checks/buildHookContentCheck.unit.test.ts` and `tests/unit-testing/42-test-mock-wrapper-untyped/check.unit.test.ts`. Neither suite is touched by this phase (nor by phases 1 and 3), neither imports anything this phase changed, and the whole run finished in 2.55s across 104 suites, which points at jest worker instability under parallel ts compilation rather than at the diff. I re-read the full diff and confirmed it compiles and is self-consistent (imports present, bundle regenerated and matching source), but I could not re-run the suite to confirm the flake: the granted-commands section allows `pnpm` only for producing plan deliverables and explicitly forbids using it to verify. If the gate reproduces the same two SIGSEGVs on re-run, the cause is the pack's jest worker configuration, not this phase.

The two tests this assignment calls for were already present, uncommitted, in the working tree and matched the plan's specified names and assertions exactly. Rather than rewrite healthy tests or duplicate them, I audited them for tautological assertions (specifically whether toMatchObject with a Map expectation actually constrains the map) and reported complete with an empty changedFiles list. If the pipeline expects a worker invocation to always produce a diff, this run will look like a no-op.

The plan specifies test edits only for buildImportGraphInput.unit.test.ts and the two testkit/pack test files, and says nothing about coverage through runPackageChecks or validateStandardsPack — the two subjects assigned to me. I chose to extend the existing runPackageChecks.checkInputs.unit.test.ts scenario file (the file that already pins what each input kind arrives carrying) rather than create a new scenario suite, and to add one import-graph case to validateStandardsPack, which had no import-graph coverage at all before this change even though it is the second caller of buildCheckInput.

To prove buildCheckInput actually forwards packagesDir rather than the builder defaulting it, I added a second test running with packagesDir: 'modules'. The plan's own test only exercises the default 'packages', which would still pass if the configured value were dropped somewhere between runPackageChecks and readPackageDependencies.

packages/engine/src/standardsCheck/common/checkInputs/ holds dedicated *.unit.test.ts files for every builder — internals under a module common/, which the module-boundary testing standard classifies as migration debt. The plan directs new coverage into one of them (buildImportGraphInput.unit.test.ts), while my assignment forbids testing non-subjects. I left those files untouched and drove all new coverage through the two subjects; flagging the directory as a migration candidate rather than acting on it.

The verification gate failed on a non-deterministic jest worker SIGSEGV (`A jest worker process (pid=89609) was terminated by another process: signal=SIGSEGV`) in packages/standards-typescript, in a suite unrelated to this task's subjects and changed internals. Zero tests failed. Because the role forbids running tests, a re-invoked agent cannot reproduce, confirm, or mitigate a crash like this — its only honest move is to re-audit and hand the same tests back. Two things would help: (1) the gate distinguishing 'suite failed to run / worker died' from 'assertions failed' before re-invoking a test agent, ideally retrying the crashed suite once with --runInBand; (2) the failure excerpt naming which package's gate crashed relative to the agent's subject list, since here the crashed suite is in a package that holds none of them.

Role rules cover 'fix your tests' and 'report failed if it traces to a source defect', but not the third case that actually occurred: the failure traces to neither. I chose status `complete` with the diagnosis in `summary` rather than `failed`, since `failures` is documented as naming a suspected source defect and there is no defect to name — the tests are correct and the crash is environmental.
